content: 1. A study conducted in South Africa highlights the urgent need to address early cessation of breastfeeding among women to improve child health outcomes. The research emphasizes the importance of interventions to support sustained breastfeeding practices. 2. Research in rural Zimbabwe demonstrates that heat treatment of expressed breast milk is a viable feeding option for HIV-exposed but uninfected children after six months of age. This approach provides a safe alternative for mothers living with HIV to continue providing breast milk while minimizing the risk of HIV transmission. 3. A cross-sectional survey in Gaborone, Botswana, explored the knowledge, attitudes, and practices of HIV-infected pregnant women regarding infant feeding. The study primarily focused on the intention to breastfeed but did not provide data on whether exclusive breastfeeding was practiced. 4. A randomized controlled trial in a poor urban setting in Kenya assessed the impact of counseling on exclusive breastfeeding practices. The study population did not include HIV-infected individuals, and the outcomes were specific to exclusive breastfeeding promotion. 5. A community-based assessment in rural Zimbabwe evaluated infant feeding practices within a program aimed at preventing mother-to-child HIV transmission. However, the study did not specifically examine exclusive breastfeeding for six months or early initiation of breastfeeding, nor did it test specific interventions. 6. A study in South Africa examined the relationship between infant feeding, HIV transmission, and mortality at 18 months. The findings underscore the need for mothers to make informed feeding choices and for programs to prioritize appropriate support. However, the study did not test interventions to promote exclusive breastfeeding. 7. The Zambia Exclusive Breastfeeding Study discussed the design challenges of a clinical trial involving behavioral interventions. The study provided a rationale for future research but was not a clinical trial itself. 8. A Lancet article reviewed the prevention of mother-to-child HIV transmission in the context of achieving health-related Millennium Development Goals. The study did not address exclusive breastfeeding or test relevant interventions. 9. A cross-sectional survey in Botswana examined the knowledge, attitudes, and practices of HIV-infected pregnant women regarding infant feeding. The study reported outcomes related to the decision to breastfeed but did not confirm whether exclusive breastfeeding occurred. 10. The Kesho Bora Study evaluated the safety and effectiveness of antiretroviral drugs during pregnancy, delivery, and breastfeeding to prevent mother-to-child HIV transmission. The study did not test interventions to promote exclusive breastfeeding. 11. A study in Zimbabwe assessed the adoption of safer infant feeding and postpartum sexual practices in relation to maternal HIV status. The research compared the costs of different antiretroviral options but did not focus on exclusive breastfeeding. 12. A model-based analysis in Zimbabwe explored the feasibility of achieving WHO target rates for mother-to-child HIV transmission. The study did not test interventions or outcomes related to exclusive breastfeeding. 13. Research in Nigeria examined the social determinants of mixed feeding behavior among HIV-infected mothers. The study did not address interventions to promote exclusive breastfeeding. 14. A study in Ethiopia investigated infant feeding practices among HIV-positive mothers attending prevention of mother-to-child transmission clinics. The research did not address interventions to promote exclusive breastfeeding. 15. A mixed-methods study in Cape Town, South Africa, explored the diversity of influences on infant feeding strategies among women living with HIV. The study provided breastfeeding rates but did not specify whether exclusive breastfeeding was practiced. 16. A study in Tanzania identified predictors of breastfeeding cessation among HIV-infected women. The research did not address exclusive breastfeeding or early initiation of breastfeeding. 17. Research in Uganda examined the relationship between household food insecurity, maternal nutritional status, and infant feeding practices among HIV-infected women receiving antiretroviral therapy. The study did not address interventions to promote breastfeeding. 18. A study in Kenya explored the implications of HIV serostatus disclosure on infant feeding practices. The research did not address interventions to promote exclusive breastfeeding. 19. A study in Kenya reviewed the relationship between maternal demographics and breastfeeding behavior among HIV-positive women. The research focused on maternal characteristics rather than interventions to promote exclusive breastfeeding. 20. A study in Uganda investigated the prevalence and factors associated with exclusive breastfeeding in the context of HIV/AIDS. The research did not address interventions to promote exclusive breastfeeding. 21. Research in Nigeria examined the challenges of adherence to infant feeding choices in the prevention of mother-to-child HIV transmission. The study did not address interventions to promote exclusive breastfeeding. 22. A qualitative study in South Africa explored the experiences of HIV-positive women regarding infant feeding. The research did not address interventions or outcomes related to exclusive breastfeeding. 23. A study in Zambia examined the knowledge of primiparous mothers about mother-to-child HIV transmission. The research did not address outcomes of interest related to exclusive breastfeeding. 24. A study in Durban, South Africa, explored the experiences of breastfeeding among HIV-positive women. The research did not address outcomes of interest related to exclusive breastfeeding. 25. A study in Malawi examined the role of grandmothers in breastfeeding and complementary feeding practices. The research did not address outcomes of interest related to exclusive breastfeeding. 26. A study in Southern Africa assessed the impact of infant feeding counseling encounters. The research highlighted the need for improved training for counselors but did not address outcomes of interest. 27. A study in South Africa evaluated the context of peer counseling for infant feeding in a high HIV prevalence area. The research did not address outcomes of interest related to exclusive breastfeeding. 28. A review of site-specific interventions to improve prevention of mother-to-child HIV transmission programs highlighted qualitative program insights. The study did not address outcomes of interest related to exclusive breastfeeding. 29. A study in resource-poor settings reflected on informed choice in infant feeding. The research did not provide data on interventions or outcomes of interest. 30. A longitudinal qualitative study in South Africa examined infant feeding decision-making among HIV-positive women. The research did not provide information on interventions of interest. 31. A study in South Africa explored the impact of the HIV epidemic on infant feeding practices. The research did not assess the association between interventions and outcomes of interest. 32. A study in South Africa assessed the barriers to HIV disclosure among women enrolled in prevention of mother-to-child transmission programs. The research evaluated barriers but did not address interventions to promote exclusive breastfeeding. 33. A study in resource-poor communities assessed knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding infant feeding options among HIV-positive mothers. The research did not provide data on outcomes of interest. 34. A study in South Africa evaluated mothers' perceptions and experiences of infant feeding within a peer counseling intervention. The research did not address outcomes of interest. 35. A study in Zambia examined the determinants of infant feeding choices among mothers. The research was unable to determine the percentage of the population that received feeding interventions or practiced exclusive breastfeeding. 36. A study in Burkina Faso, Cambodia, and Cameroon explored counseling and decision-making regarding infant feeding options. The research did not provide data on interventions or outcomes of interest. 37. A study in South Africa assessed the effect of the HIV epidemic on infant feeding practices. The research was unable to assess the association between interventions and outcomes of interest. 38. A study in South Africa evaluated the experiences of HIV-positive women regarding infant feeding. The research did not address outcomes of interest related to exclusive breastfeeding.
